`attacks` lists the techniques to run. Every goal goes through every attack, unless [`execution.escalate`](../execution.md#executionspec) says otherwise.

Every technique is listed below, and each has its own page giving its parameters and the helper models it drives.

## `attacks[]` {#attackspec}

One attack technique to run against the target: which one, how to tune it,
and which helper models it drives.

| Field | Type | Default | Description |
|---|---|---|---|
| `name` | string | **required** | The technique to run, e.g. `flipattack` or `tap`. It must be one of the registered attacks. |
| `parameters` | map of string to any | empty | The technique's own settings. Valid keys differ per attack; anything you leave out keeps its default. Each attack's page lists its parameters. |
| `roles` | map of string to [ModelConfig](../target.md#modelconfig) | empty | The helper models an adaptive attack uses, keyed by role name (for example `attacker`). Static attacks need none. Each attack's page lists the roles it requires. |

## Examples

**One static attack, which needs no helper model**

```yaml
attacks:
- name: flipattack
  parameters:
    flip_mode: FCS
```

**An adaptive attack, which drives its own attacker model**

```yaml
attacks:
- name: tap
  parameters:
    width: 4
    depth: 3
  roles:
    attacker:
      name: llama3.2
      connection:
        provider: ollama
        type: OLLAMA
    on_topic:
      name: llama3.2
      connection:
        provider: ollama
        type: OLLAMA
```


## The catalog

Every technique HackAgent can run.

**Static.** Builds its prompts up front and sends them. It drives no model of its own, so it is cheap and repeatable.

**Adaptive.** Searches: it reads the target's replies and refines its prompts, which is why it needs an attacker model.

**Multi-turn.** Holds one growing conversation with the target, escalating turn by turn.

| Attack | Kind | Needs | What it does |
|---|---|---|---|
| [AdvPrefix](advprefix.md) | Adaptive | `attacker` | Prefilling attack: opens the model's answer with an adversarial prefix and keeps the prefixes that work best. |
| [AutoDAN-Turbo](autodan_turbo.md) | Adaptive | `attacker`, `embedder`, `summarizer` | Lifelong jailbreak strategy search with warm-up and retrieval phases. |
| [Baseline](baseline.md) | Static | none | Direct goal submission without transformation (control condition). |
| [BoN](bon.md) | Adaptive | none | Best-of-N augmentation search with inline judge evaluation. |
| [CipherChat](cipherchat.md) | Static | none | Cipher-based prompt transformation with optional demonstrations. |
| [Crescendo](crescendo.md) | Multi-turn | `attacker` | Multi-turn escalation attack that gradually steers a persistent conversation toward the goal, with judge-driven backtracking on refusals. |
| [FC-Attack](fc.md) | Static | none | FC-Attack: auto-generated flowchart images to jailbreak VLMs. |
| [FlipAttack](flipattack.md) | Static | none | Prompt obfuscation via character/word flipping modes. |
| [h4rm3l](h4rm3l.md) | Static | none | Composable decorator-program attack chaining multiple obfuscations. |
| [MML](mml.md) | Static | none | Multi-Modal Linkage attack encoding harmful prompts into images for VLMs. |
| [PAIR](pair.md) | Adaptive | `attacker` | Prompt Automatic Iterative Refinement with attacker/scorer loops. |
| [PAP](pap.md) | Adaptive | `attacker` | Persuasive Adversarial Prompts using persuasion-technique taxonomies. |
| [RAG poisoning](rag.md) | Static | `attacker`, `embedder` | Indirect prompt injection via poisoned documents in a retrieval-augmented (RAG) corpus. |
| [Static Template](static_template.md) | Static | none | Template-based static template jailbreak attack. |
| [TAP](tap.md) | Adaptive | `attacker` | Tree of Attacks with Pruning search attack. |
| [tFC-Attack](tfc.md) | Static | none | tFC-Attack: text-only flowchart encoding attack for any LLM (DOT, Mermaid, TikZ, PlantUML, ASCII). |
| [Tool-output IPI](tool_output_ipi.md) | Adaptive | none | Indirect prompt injection via poisoned tool observations (InjecAgent / OPI). |

:::tip[Where these come from]

Each attack follows a published paper or reference implementation. Parameter defaults follow the paper unless the description says otherwise, which happens when a value assumes local model weights rather than an API endpoint.

:::
